analysis.one_liner: Bans hidden PBM pricing markups in Medicaid and forces pharmacy benefit managers to disclose and justify their fees in Medicare.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill with 27 cosponsors, led by the Finance chairman and the top committee Democrat, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since its December 2025 introduction with no action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and pay pharmacies for insurers and government health programs. In Medicaid, it bans 'spread pricing' (where a PBM charges the state more than it pays the pharmacy and keeps the difference) and requires pharmacies' actual drug costs to be surveyed and published. In Medicare, it forces PBMs to disclose their revenues and affiliate relationships, pay them only flat, fair-market service fees, let any willing pharmacy join drug plan networks, and set up an enforcement process pharmacies can use against unfair contract terms. It also funds oversight studies by the Inspector General and GAO.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid patients, who pay less for prescriptions when middleman markups are stripped out; independent and community pharmacies, including the sole pharmacy in a small town, which get reimbursement tied to their actual drug costs and protection from one-sided PBM contracts; and state Medicaid programs, which lose federal matching funds if their contracts allow spread pricing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare and Medicaid patients and community pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: In Medicaid, payment must be a transparent pass-through limited to the drug's ingredient cost plus a dispensing fee, with PBM administrative pay capped at fair market value — spread pricing is disallowed for federal matching purposes [S2].

Pharmacies' actual drug acquisition costs must be surveyed monthly and the results made public, with civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation for pharmacies that refuse or falsify survey responses [S2].

In Medicare Part D, PBMs and their affiliates may keep only bona fide flat-dollar service fees not based on drug price, rebates, or formulary placement, and must disgorge anything else they collected [S2].

Prescription drug plans must allow any willing pharmacy that meets standard terms into their networks, and the Secretary must set 'reasonable and relevant' standards for PBM-pharmacy contracts, with an allegation process and anti-retaliation protections so pharmacies can report violations without fear [S2].

PBMs must file detailed annual reports covering revenues retained, the share of prescriptions steered to PBM-owned pharmacies, generic-versus-brand formulary decisions, and payments to brokers and consultants, and sponsors may audit them annually [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers — chiefly the three big firms (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum Rx) — lose the spread between what they charge plans and what they pay pharmacies, and lose price-based compensation in Medicare; their affiliated mail-order and specialty pharmacies lose the built-in advantage of steering. Drug manufacturers face new disclosure of rebate contracts. Federal spending rises by roughly $327 million for enforcement, surveys, and oversight studies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliate pharmacies

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates about $327 million for fiscal 2026 to CMS, the Inspector General, and the Medicaid cost survey, plus $9 million a year thereafter, adding to federal health program administrative costs [S2].

It does not ban manufacturer rebates — it allows them so long as they are fully passed through to the plan — so the rebate-driven system that keeps drug list prices inflated stays in place; the middleman is regulated rather than removed [S2].

Plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers face heavy new reporting and audit obligations, and critics of such rules argue the compliance burden and loss of pricing flexibility can be passed on through premiums — an honest supporter would acknowledge premiums could absorb some transition cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: it attacks a documented middleman practice — being paid more than it pays the pharmacy, and fees that scale with drug price — that raises costs for state Medicaid programs, Medicare beneficiaries, and independent pharmacies, and it does so with enforcement teeth (disgorgement, penalties, anti-retaliation) rather than just disclosure. The main honest weaknesses are that it leaves the manufacturer rebate system intact and carries a meaningful administrative price tag; the transparency and fee reforms outweigh both, but the rebate loophole limits how much list prices will actually fall.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 4, 2025 with 27 bipartisan cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 4, 2025 by Senator Mike Crapo with 21 original cosponsors and read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S4].
It has gathered 27 cosponsors total — 15 of 55 Senate Republicans and 12 of 45 Senate Democrats [S3].
Its sponsor, Mike Crapo, chairs the Senate Finance Committee, the same committee the bill was referred to, and Ron Wyden, the committee's ranking Democrat, is an original cosponsor [S1].
No markup, hearing, or floor action appears in the action history; the bill sits in committee with no vote taken [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome has been reached, so no one has gained or lost yet. If the bill continues to sit, pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliated pharmacies benefit most from the delay, since the current pricing system stays in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill awaits committee action

for.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
for.role: Senate Finance Committee Chairman; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and referred it to his own Finance Committee, which controls its fate.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor alongside the chairman when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
against.role: Industry with a direct financial stake in current PBM pricing
against.what_they_did: No action specific to this bill appears in the record; major PBMs have publicly opposed comparable PBM reform measures.

sides.party_line_note: Support is bipartisan across the whole bill: 15 of 55 Senate Republicans and 12 of 45 Senate Democrats are cosponsors, led jointly by the Finance chairman and ranking Democrat.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: Spread pricing is banned in Medicaid — PBM payment must pass through to pharmacies in full with only a fair-market admin fee — and in Medicare, PBMs may keep only flat, price-independent service fees and must disgorge anything else, with detailed annual disclosure of revenue retained and affiliate steering. These are the core profit engines of the PBM model.

Reimbursement will be based on surveyed actual acquisition costs made public monthly, drug plans must accept any willing pharmacy, and pharmacies gain an enforcement process, anti-retaliation protections, and audit rights against one-sided PBM contract terms.

Affiliate pharmacies must be identified in surveys and reports, and PBMs must disclose the share of prescriptions steered to their own pharmacies and the pricing advantage they get — removing the structural edge that pushes volume to PBM-owned dispensers.

industries.industry: Medicare drug plan sponsors (PDP and MA-PD insurers)
industries.note: Sponsors gain financially — PBMs must reimburse them for penalties and disgorge improper remuneration — but they take on certification, audit, and reporting duties and lose PBM pricing flexibility that could show up as modest premium pressure.

Manufacturer rebates remain lawful if fully passed through to the plan, so the rebate system survives, but rebate and discount contracts with PBMs — including those conditioned on formulary placement — must be explained in writing within 30 days.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has strong bipartisan backing on the very committee that controls it, which puts it ahead of most newly referred bills. But no markup or hearing is scheduled, and with major PBM reform measures already moving elsewhere, its realistic path is a Finance Committee markup and possible attachment to a larger health or Medicare package if leadership prioritizes it; without that, it most likely waits out the session without a vote.
